question: Inherited hyperammonemia is a result of deficiency of which enzyme of Krebs-Henseleit urea cycle?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "N-acetyl glutamate synthetase deficiency" -> "decreased N-acetylglutamate" -> "reduced activation of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I" -> "impaired urea cycle" -> "accumulation of ammonia" -> "hyperammonemia" -> 95%

analysis: Inherited hyperammonemia is commonly associated with deficiencies in enzymes of the urea cycle. The urea cycle, also known as the Krebs-Henseleit cycle, involves several key enzymes, including carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I, ornithine transcarbamylase, argininosuccinate synthetase, argininosuccinate lyase, and arginase. N-acetyl glutamate synthetase is not directly part of the urea cycle but is crucial for its regulation, as it produces N-acetylglutamate, an essential activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I. Deficiency in N-acetyl glutamate synthetase can lead to hyperammonemia due to impaired activation of the urea cycle. The other enzymes listed (malate dehydrogenase, isocitrate dehydrogenase, and succinate dehydrogenase) are part of the citric acid cycle, not the urea cycle. Therefore, the most likely correct answer is N-acetyl glutamate synthetase.
